newsitem.title: USA: NYH spot gasoline jumps on keen demand, low stocks.
newsitem.headline: NYH spot gasoline jumps on keen demand, low stocks.

text.p: East Coast spot gasoline prices gathered strength Thursday afternoon amid record low U.S. stocks and potent demand, players said a day after Tosco and other refiners snapped up big parcels in New York Harbor(NYH).

"It's still going strong and there's some more room on the upside," one trader said, adding NYH conventional unleaded "M5" winter-grade sold for three cents over December futures, -- about 0.40 cent firmer than Wednesday differentials.
December futures prices were hovering about 0.20 cent over the print at the NYMEX close, putting cash "M5" values at about 66.80 cents a gallon.
Prompt NYH "A5" winter-grade reformulated gasoline was offered at a lofty 3.50 cents over the print, almost one cent a gallon higher than at the beginning of the week.
Traders said they were still trying to sort out why Tosco Corp unexpectedly stepped up to buy big parcels of "M5" and "A5" grades in NYH on Wednesday afternoon.

Although they initially pegged Tosco's purchases in the 500,000-barrel range, some said the actual volume now seems to have been half of that, with Global Petroleum, Citgo Petroleum and Mobil Corp each picking up 100,000 barrels or more.
"Even 200,000 barrels for Tosco is a significant purchase. The fact they were that short is surprising," one trader said, adding the independent refiner was not seen back in the market on Thursday.
Other traders speculated Tosco may have bought barrels to tweak NYMEX futures prices higher, noting its giant 290,000 barrel per day Bayway refinery in Linden, New Jersey, stood to benefit.

But one player said if Tosco was really trying to move the gasoline markets, it would have stepped up for all eyes to see rather than placing orders "quietly" through a Florida-based trader. Tosco declined to comment, citing company policy.

There were no indications that the Bayway refinery was having problems, but one trader said any major output snag at an East Coast refinery could push prices "a nickel or a dime higher" (five to 10 cents) given record low U.S. stocks. The East Coast refines only a third of the gasoline it uses.
"We've got record low U.S. gasoline stocks for this time of year," said Jim Lockhart, senior analyst for American Petroleum Institute.

"They are the lowest, in fact, we've seen in any month in the last several decades," he added, pegging current primary inventories at about 191 million barrels -- compared with almost 197 last year and over 200 million for previous years in late October.
